de Vries PJ.role: Co-author of the EXIST-3 everolimus seizure trial and of the TRON trial of everolimus for neuropsychological problems in tuberous sclerosis complex.
de Vries PJ.sub: Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Cape Town · listed on two Atlas papers, 2016 and 2026
story: Petrus J de Vries is a middle author on two human trials in the Atlas, both in people with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), a genetic condition in which mTOR is switched on too much. PubMed lists him at the Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Cape Town, on both papers.

EXIST-3 (2016) was a phase 3 trial in 366 people with TSC and seizures that other drugs had not controlled. Adding everolimus cut seizure frequency more than placebo, and the higher dose did best. The TRON trial (2026) looked at thinking and behaviour in 38 people. Everolimus did not clearly beat placebo there, because both groups improved a lot. Two other EXIST papers in the Atlas list the same name, but their PubMed records give no affiliation, so they are not covered here.

highlights.FRE2016: Middle author of the EXIST-3 phase 3 trial of everolimus for treatment-resistant seizures in tuberous sclerosis, listed at the University of Cape Town.
highlights.SAX2026: Middle author of the TRON randomised trial, which found no clear everolimus benefit over placebo on neuropsychological measures in tuberous sclerosis.

de Vries PJ.lab_name: Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Cape Town (Cape Town, South Africa)

Glass DJ.role: Co-author of two Novartis trials of mTOR inhibitors given to older adults to see if immune function improves.
Glass DJ.sub: Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research, Cambridge, MA · listed on two Atlas papers, 2014 and 2018
story: David J. Glass is a middle author on two human trials in the Atlas, both from Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Both asked whether a short, low-dose course of an mTOR inhibitor can help the aging immune system.

In the 2014 study, older volunteers took everolimus before a flu shot and their antibody response rose by about 20 percent. In the 2018 phase 2a trial of 264 older adults, a low-dose combination of two mTOR inhibitors was linked to fewer reported infections over the next year. A later, larger trial of one of the drugs did not confirm a clinical benefit. Two 2001 muscle papers in the Atlas list a D J Glass, but PubMed gives only initials there, so they are not covered here.

highlights.MAN2014: Middle author of the trial showing that everolimus raised the flu-vaccine response by about 20 percent in older volunteers.
highlights.MAN2018: Middle author of the phase 2a trial linking low-dose TORC1 inhibition to fewer infections in 264 older adults.

Glass DJ.lab_name: Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)

Caccamo A.role: First author of a 2010 study in Alzheimer's disease model mice linking mTOR, amyloid-beta and Tau.
Caccamo A.sub: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio
story: Antonella Caccamo was first author of a 2010 mouse study from the Department of Physiology at the University of Texas Health Science Center in San Antonio. It asked how mTOR, amyloid-beta and Tau fit together in Alzheimer's disease.

The work found a loop. Amyloid-beta raises mTOR activity, and high mTOR blocks autophagy, the cell's clean-up process, so amyloid and Tau build up further. In a mouse model of the disease, rapamycin broke the loop, improved memory and lowered both amyloid and Tau. Blocking autophagy removed the amyloid benefit. This was done in mice, not in people. Caccamo also appears in a 2012 Atlas paper, but PubMed gives no affiliation for that record, so it is not covered here.

highlights.CAC2010: First author of the mouse study showing that rapamycin rescued memory and lowered amyloid-beta and Tau through autophagy.

Caccamo A.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center (San Antonio, Texas, USA)

Cao ZL.role: First author of a 2026 review of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome and substrate-selective mTORC1 control.
Cao ZL.sub: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Wenzhou Medical University
story: Zhi-Lie Cao was first author of a 2026 review article in Frontiers in Oncology. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Urology at Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, which is affiliated with Wenzhou Medical University, and also at a hospital in Hangzhou.

The review looks at Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, a genetic condition caused by loss of the FLCN gene. It argues that the old picture of mTORC1 simply being switched on everywhere does not fit. FLCN acts on RagC/D, so mTORC1 control is selective. Losing both gene copies drives kidney tumours, while having only one working copy is enough to cause lung and skin problems. Being a review, it reports no new experiments.

highlights.CAO2026: First author of the review reframing Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome around substrate-selective mTORC1 control and gene dosage.

Cao ZL.lab_name: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province Affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University (Taizhou, China)

Chen WY.role: Last author of a 2026 review of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome and substrate-selective mTORC1 control.
Chen WY.sub: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Wenzhou Medical University
story: Wei-Ying Chen was last author of a 2026 review in Frontiers in Oncology on Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Urology at Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated with Wenzhou Medical University.

The review proposes that FLCN, the gene lost in this syndrome, controls mTORC1 in a selective way rather than switching it on everywhere. It links loss of both FLCN copies to kidney tumours and loss of one copy to lung and skin changes. It is a review of existing work, not a new experiment.

highlights.CAO2026: Last author of the review on gene dosage and substrate-selective mTORC1 regulation in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome.

Chen WY.lab_name: Department of Urology, Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province Affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University (Taizhou, China)

Cao P.role: First author of a 2026 study of dihydromyricetin in hypertrophic scar.
Cao P.sub: Burn & Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University, Wuxi
story: Peng Cao was first author of a 2026 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology. PubMed lists the author at the Burn & Trauma Treatment Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University in Wuxi.

The team tested dihydromyricetin, a plant compound, on hypertrophic scar. In scar-derived fibroblasts and in a rabbit ear scar model, it lowered collagen and other scar markers, and AKT and mTOR phosphorylation fell at the same time. The authors state that this does not prove the drug works through that pathway.

highlights.CAO2026B: First author of the cell and rabbit study in which dihydromyricetin reduced scar markers alongside lower AKT and mTOR phosphorylation.

Cao P.lab_name: Burn & Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China)

Lyu G.role: Last author of a 2026 study of dihydromyricetin in hypertrophic scar.
Lyu G.sub: Burn & Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University, Wuxi
story: Guozhong Lyu was last author of a 2026 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology. PubMed lists the author at the Burn & Trauma Treatment Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University in Wuxi, and at a national emergency medical research center in Beijing.

The study found that dihydromyricetin lowered scar-related markers in hypertrophic scar fibroblasts and improved scars in a rabbit ear model. AKT and mTOR phosphorylation dropped along with it, but the authors say cause and effect were not shown.

highlights.CAO2026B: Last author of the study in which dihydromyricetin improved hypertrophic scar features in cells and rabbits.

Lyu G.lab_name: Burn & Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China)

Lovat P.role: Middle author of two Newcastle University studies on mTORC1, senescence and mitophagy.
Lovat P.sub: Translation and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2024
story: Penny Lovat is a middle author on two cell-biology papers in the Atlas, both from groups at Newcastle University. PubMed lists her in the Institute of Cellular Medicine in 2017 and in the Translation and Clinical Research Institute in 2024.

The 2017 paper explains why mTORC1 stays active in senescent human cells even when nutrients are removed. The 2024 paper shows that healthy human cells clear damaged mitochondria all the time, that this stops in senescent and aged cells, and that restarting it with a small molecule improved markers of aging in cells. Both studies used cultured cells.

highlights.CAR2017: Middle author of the study showing mTORC1 stays active in senescent human fibroblasts because of upstream sensing defects.
highlights.KEL2024: Middle author of the study showing that suppressed basal mitophagy drives cellular aging features that a p62-targeting molecule could reverse.

Lovat P.lab_name: Precision Medicine, Translation and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, UK)

Nelson G.role: Co-author of two Newcastle University studies on mTORC1, senescence and mitophagy.
Nelson G.sub: Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2024
story: Glyn Nelson is a co-author on two cell-biology papers in the Atlas, both from Newcastle University. PubMed lists him at the Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences in 2017 and the Biosciences Institute in 2024. He is second author on the 2017 paper and a middle author on the 2024 one.

The 2017 paper found that mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent human fibroblasts and no longer responds to nutrient removal. The 2024 paper found that routine clearing of damaged mitochondria shuts down in senescent and aged cells. Both were done in cultured human cells.

highlights.CAR2017: Second author of the study showing mTORC1 stays active in senescent human fibroblasts.
highlights.KEL2024: Middle author of the study linking suppressed basal mitophagy to cellular aging phenotypes.

Nelson G.lab_name: Biosciences Institute, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, UK)

Castilho RM.role: First author of a 2009 mouse study on Wnt, mTOR and epidermal stem cell exhaustion.
Castilho RM.sub: Oral and Pharyngeal Cancer Branch, NIDCR, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda
story: Rogerio M Castilho was first author of a 2009 paper in Cell Stem Cell. PubMed lists the author in the Oral and Pharyngeal Cancer Branch of the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the US National Institutes of Health.

In mice, constant Wnt signalling first made hair follicles grow fast, then wore out the skin stem cells and caused hair loss. This depended on mTOR, and rapamycin rescued the effect. The study suggests mTOR can push stem cells into senescence when growth signals never stop. It was done in mice.

highlights.CAS2009: First author of the mouse study showing that Wnt-driven mTOR activity exhausts epidermal stem cells and that rapamycin rescues this.

Castilho RM.lab_name: Oral and Pharyngeal Cancer Branch, National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)

Castellano BM.role: First author of a 2017 study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1.
Castellano BM.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley
story: Brian M Castellano was first author of a 2017 paper in Science. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley.

The study showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, is a signal that helps switch on mTORC1. A protein called SLC38A9 is needed for this, and it works separately from its role in sensing the amino acid arginine. Another protein, NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The work was done in cultured cells.

highlights.CAS2017: First author of the study showing that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9 and NPC1.

Castellano BM.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)

Covey DF.role: Co-author of two Berkeley studies on how lysosomal cholesterol feeds into mTORC1.
Covey DF.sub: Department of Developmental Biology and Biochemistry, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2022
story: Douglas F Covey is a middle author on two Science papers from the Zoncu group at Berkeley, listed in PubMed at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis both times. Both papers are about cholesterol as a signal to mTORC1 in cultured cells.

The 2017 paper showed that cholesterol in the lysosome activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2022 paper identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and passes the signal on by holding back the GATOR1 complex.

highlights.CAS2017: Middle author of the study showing lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via SLC38A9 and NPC1.
highlights.SHI2022: Middle author of the study identifying LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

Covey DF.lab_name: Department of Developmental Biology and Biochemistry, Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, Missouri, USA)

Davis OB.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2022
story: Oliver B Davis is a middle author on two Science papers from the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. Both are about cholesterol as a signal to mTORC1 in cultured cells.

Moldavski O.role: Co-author of two Berkeley studies on lysosomal control of mTORC1.
Moldavski O.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2018
story: Ofer Moldavski is a co-author on two papers from the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. He is third author on the 2017 paper and a middle author on the 2018 one.

The 2017 paper showed that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2018 paper described a switch in the Rag-Ragulator scaffold on the lysosome whose grip on mTORC1 changes with nutrient levels. Both are cell studies.

highlights.CAS2017: Third author of the study showing lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via SLC38A9.
highlights.LAW2018: Middle author of the study on a nutrient-controlled affinity switch in the Rag-Ragulator scaffold.

Nomura DK.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2022

story: Rushika M Perera is a middle author on two Science papers about cholesterol as a signal to mTORC1. PubMed lists her in the Department of Anatomy at the University of California, San Francisco, on both, while the first authors worked at UC Berkeley.

Thelen AM.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley · listed on two Atlas papers, 2017 and 2019
story: Ashley M Thelen is a co-author on two Science papers from the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley. She is second author on the 2017 paper and a middle author on the 2019 one.

The 2017 paper showed that lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2019 paper described, at the structural level, a checkpoint in how Rag GTPases are switched on. These are laboratory studies on cells and purified proteins.

highlights.CAS2017: Second author of the study showing lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via SLC38A9.
highlights.LAW2019: Middle author of the structural study of a Rag GTPase activation checkpoint.

Orozco JM.role: Co-author of four Whitehead Institute studies on how nutrients and mitochondrial stress signal to mTORC1.
Orozco JM.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, Cambridge, MA · listed on four Atlas papers, 2014–2021
story: Jose M Orozco is a co-author on four papers in the Atlas, all listed at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, between 2014 and 2021. PubMed shows the Whitehead Institute together with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology on the earlier papers. He is third author on the 2014 paper and a middle author on the others.

The papers cover how mTORC1 learns about its surroundings. Sestrins bind GATOR2 to dampen amino-acid signalling (2014). KICSTOR holds GATOR1 at the lysosome so nutrients can regulate mTORC1 (2017). SAMTOR senses S-adenosylmethionine, a methyl donor linked to methionine (2017). Genome-wide CRISPR screens showed that AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1 (2021). All four are cell studies.

highlights.CHA2014: Third author of the study showing Sestrins bind GATOR2 to restrain amino-acid signalling to mTORC1.
highlights.WOL2017: Middle author of the study showing KICSTOR recruits GATOR1 to the lysosome.
highlights.GU2017: Middle author of the study identifying SAMTOR as an S-adenosylmethionine sensor for mTORC1.
highlights.CON2021: Middle author of the CRISPR screen study on how mTORC1 senses mitochondrial dysfunction.

Orozco JM.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)

Spooner E.role: Co-author of two Whitehead Institute studies on amino-acid sensing upstream of mTORC1.
Spooner E.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Massachusetts Institute of Technology · listed on two Atlas papers, 2013 and 2014
story: Eric Spooner is a co-author on two papers in the Atlas, both listed at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He is a middle author on both.

The 2013 paper showed that folliculin acts as a GAP for RagC/D, helping amino acids switch on mTORC1 at the lysosome. The 2014 paper showed that Sestrins bind GATOR2 to dampen the amino-acid signal. Both are cell studies. A third Atlas paper from 2007 lists the same name, but its PubMed record gives no affiliation for him, so it is not covered here.

highlights.TSU2013: Middle author of the study showing folliculin is a GAP for RagC/D in amino-acid signalling to mTORC1.
highlights.CHA2014: Middle author of the study showing Sestrins bind GATOR2 to restrain amino-acid signalling to mTORC1.

Spooner E.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)

Chen Xizi.role: First author of the 2018 cryo-EM structure of human mTOR complex 2.
Chen Xizi.sub: Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Shanghai Medical College
story: Xizi Chen was first author of a 2018 paper in Cell Research. PubMed lists the author at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and at other Fudan University units in Shanghai.

The team used cryo-electron microscopy to work out the 3D shape of human mTORC2 at 4.9 angstrom resolution. The structure showed how the Rictor and mSin1 subunits sit around mTOR and block rapamycin from binding, which explains why mTORC2 is insensitive to rapamycin. This was a structural study of purified protein.

highlights.CHE2018: First author of the cryo-EM study of human mTORC2 that explained its rapamycin insensitivity.

Chen Xizi.lab_name: Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Shanghai Medical College of Fudan University (Shanghai, China)

Chen K.role: First author of a 2026 study of engineered exosomes, AMPK/mTOR signalling and wound healing.
Chen K.sub: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University
story: Kewei Chen was first author of a 2026 paper in Cellular Signalling. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Plastic Surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University.

The study tested exosomes, tiny vesicles released by stem cells, that were engineered to carry FGF21. In skin fibroblasts and in a mouse wound model, they sped up wound closure. They raised AMPK activity, lowered mTOR signalling and boosted glycolysis in the fibroblasts.

highlights.CHEN2026: First author of the cell and mouse study of FGF21-loaded exosomes that promoted wound healing through AMPK/mTOR signalling.

Chen K.lab_name: Department of Plastic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Wenzhou, China)

Chen Xianglong.role: First author of a 2026 study linking impaired chaperone-mediated autophagy to mTORC1 activation in intervertebral disc degeneration.
Chen Xianglong.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
story: Xianglong Chen was first author of a 2026 paper in Advanced Science. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Orthopedics at Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.

The study looked at degeneration of the discs between the vertebrae. In disc cells from patients and in rat models, a clean-up pathway called chaperone-mediated autophagy was weakened. A protein called midnolin then built up, destroyed TSC2 and switched mTORC1 on, which drove cell senescence and tissue breakdown. Blocking midnolin, restoring the pathway or giving rapamycin reduced the damage in cells and rats.

highlights.CHEN2026C: First author of the study tracing disc degeneration to midnolin-driven loss of TSC2 and mTORC1 activation.

Chen Xianglong.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, China)

Chung CL.role: First author of a 2019 randomised trial of topical rapamycin in human skin.
Chung CL.sub: Department of Dermatology, Drexel University College of Medicine, Philadelphia
story: Christina Lee Chung was first author of a 2019 paper in GeroScience. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Dermatology at Drexel University College of Medicine in Philadelphia.

This was a small, exploratory, placebo-controlled trial in people over 40 with sun-aged skin. Thirty-six people enrolled and 17 finished. Rapamycin applied to the skin lowered the senescence marker p16 and raised collagen VII, and some participants showed visible improvement. Because the trial was small, it is early evidence only.

highlights.CHU2019: First author of the human trial in which topical rapamycin lowered p16 and raised collagen VII in skin.

Chung CL.lab_name: Department of Dermatology, Drexel University College of Medicine (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)

Correia-Melo C.role: First author of a 2018 mouse study of rapamycin in mice with enhanced NF-kB activity.
Correia-Melo C.sub: Newcastle University Institute for Ageing, Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences
story: Clara Correia-Melo was first author of a 2018 paper in Aging Cell. PubMed lists the author at the Newcastle University Institute for Ageing and the Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences at Newcastle University.

The team gave rapamycin to mice with genetically raised NF-kB activity, which develop low-grade inflammation and age early. Rapamycin did not lengthen life or reduce inflammation. It did reduce frailty and improved memory, coordination and tissue structure, and senescence markers fell. The result suggests that healthspan benefits of rapamycin can be separate from its anti-inflammatory effect, at least in these mice.

highlights.COR2018: First author of the mouse study showing rapamycin improved healthspan without reducing inflammaging in nfkb1-null mice.

Correia-Melo C.lab_name: Newcastle University Institute for Ageing, Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, UK)

Chresta CM.role: First author of the 2009 paper describing AZD8055, an ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor.
Chresta CM.sub: AstraZeneca, Cheshire, UK (as listed by PubMed on the AZD8055 paper)
story: Christine M Chresta was first author of a 2009 paper in Cancer Research. PubMed lists the author at AstraZeneca in Cheshire, UK.

The paper describes AZD8055, a drug that blocks the mTOR kinase directly and so inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2, including outputs that rapamycin leaves untouched. It was tested in cancer cells and in mouse tumour models, where it slowed growth. Chresta is also listed on a 2009 Dundee paper in the Atlas, but PubMed gives no affiliation for that record, so it is not covered here.

highlights.CHR2009: First author of the study describing AZD8055 as a selective ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor with antitumour activity in cells and mice.

Cosulich S.role: Co-author of the 2016 Nature paper on a third-generation mTOR inhibitor that overcomes resistance mutations.
Cosulich S.sub: AstraZeneca, Alderley Park, Macclesfield, Cheshire, UK (as listed by PubMed on the 2016 paper)
story: Sabina Cosulich is a middle author of a 2016 paper in Nature. PubMed lists her at AstraZeneca in Alderley Park, Macclesfield, UK, while the first authors were at Memorial Sloan Kettering and UCSF.

The study found how cancer cells become resistant to mTOR kinase inhibitors, through mutations that raise mTOR's own activity. It then built RapaLink-1, a bivalent third-generation inhibitor that still works against those mutants in cells and mice. A 2009 AZD8055 paper in the Atlas lists the same name, but its PubMed record gives no affiliation, so it is not covered here.

highlights.ROD2016: Middle author of the study that developed RapaLink-1 to overcome mTOR resistance mutations.
